plan.title: Board ramp into a pail

items.name: Riser box
items.why: Added riser that lifts the book. The board can then end above the bucket's rim and the balls drop in.

items.why: The thick book that props up the board's high end

items.name: Cutting board ramp
items.why: Stands in for the wooden cutting board as a fixed wooden ramp. Its legs hold the low end 14 cm up, just above the bucket rim.

items.name: Cue ball
items.why: The cream cue ball at the top of the board

items.name: Golf ball
items.why: The golf ball at the top, just ahead of the cue ball

items.why: The small galvanised pail, sized as in the photo. It stands just past the board's low end to catch the balls.

goals.label: The cue ball lands in the bucket

plan.notes: Both balls are let go at the top of the board and roll down the 11° slope. They leave its low end, 14 cm up, at about 1.2 m/s and drop about 13 cm further on into the pail. The tuner may slide the pail to where they really land.
assumptions: Scale set from the golf ball (4.3 cm) and the cue ball (5.7 cm). The pail is about 13 cm wide and 12 cm deep, about 3× the golf ball, so the catalog bucket was shrunk to match.
The book is set 6 cm thick as it looks in the photo.
The scene is laid out in the motion plane: the high end is on the left and the balls roll to the right towards the pail.
The pail's bounce was lowered (its look is unchanged) so the balls do not spring back out of such a small pail.
differences: Cutting board: built as a fixed wooden plank of the same size (about 62 × 30 × 3 cm), because a loose board cannot stay propped with one end in the air. It has no juice groove.
To make it work, the board's low end no longer rests on the table. It is held 14 cm up on legs, above the 12 cm rim, so the balls drop into the pail instead of hitting its side.
To keep the board sloping downhill with its low end raised, the book now sits on an added cardboard box.
The pail stands in line with the board's end rather than beside its corner, because all motion is in one plane.
